svg.aria-label: Diagram: the four levels a Google Cloud IAM binding can sit at, what each inspection method shows and hides, a terminating procedure for tracing why a principal has access to a resource, and the redundant-binding trap that makes a deletion appear to work
svg.title: Tracing access: four levels, three tools that answer different questions, one procedure that terminates
svg.text: “Is this principal in this policy” and “can this principal act here” are different questions.
Almost every access investigation that goes wrong went wrong by treating the first as an answer to the second.
Four levels a binding can sit at
Organization
inherited by ALL resources under it
Folder
nests, so several may contribute
Project
a trust boundary — most grants land here
Resource
topics, instances, buckets, tables
Effective access is the union of all four. Nothing subtracts.
What each tool hides
get-iam-policy on the resource
does not show roles gained by inheritance
asset search-all-iam-policies
only principals granted the role DIRECTLY
the Google Cloud console
the documented way to view inherited roles
The one question where the console beats the API
#32 and #33 both ran the other way: the console hid the better option, or set a version flag you could not see.
Here it inverts — a team standardised on the CLI will systematically miss inherited grants.
A procedure that terminates
1. get-ancestors — prints the folder and organization hierarchy. This is what tells you when you are FINISHED.
2. Expand the principal into a set: itself, its groups, and their groups.
3. Read the policy at EVERY level — asking for version 3, or conditions go missing (#33).
4. Collect every binding matching any member of the set; note which level each came from.
5. Reduce: which binding actually confers it, and which are redundant against a wider inherited role?
Why step 5 matters: the fix that looks like it worked
Editor at the project, Viewer on a topic beneath it. The Viewer grant is redundant — Editor already contains it.
Asked to remove their read access, you delete the Viewer binding. The topic policy no longer names them.
They still read the topic. The deletion succeeded, the diff looks right, the access is intact.
And the better your IAM, the further the answer sits from the resource
Bind groups not users (#31) → the account appears in no binding at all; searching for it returns nothing.
Grant at a sensible level → the binding is nowhere near the object you are investigating.
Tidy IAM is harder to trace, not easier. Treat tracing as a procedure, not a lookup.
One more silent narrowing: without iam.roles.get, the search lists fewer permissions than exist — incomplete, not wrong.
None of these tools is lying. Each invites a conclusion it does not support, and none says so in its output.
